title: Online Is a Safe Space in War
author: Ubell, Robert
summary: Robert Ubell, vice dean emeritus of NYU's Tandon School of Engineering and a pioneer in online education, reflects on how digital learning -- originally designed for remote workers, home-bound patients, and rural families -- has taken on an unanticipated role: keeping education alive in wartime. Following US and Israeli military operations, universities in conflict zones found themselves unable to hold in-person classes, and online platforms became the medium through which students and faculty maintained continuity amid missiles and drones. Ubell writes from personal experience as an early architect of online education infrastructure, noting that nobody who designed these systems envisioned them as refuges from war. The article examines both the practical mechanics of wartime remote education and the psychological dimension: online spaces offer students a form of cognitive and social safety when physical campuses are inaccessible or dangerous. The piece is a meditation on the unexpected resilience and reach of digital learning, and on the human need for education even in the most extreme circumstances.
points: Online education, designed for remote workers, caregivers, and rural students, has unexpectedly become the primary mechanism for maintaining educational continuity in wartime -- a use case its architects never anticipated.

Following US and Israeli military operations, universities in conflict zones kept classes running through digital platforms while students navigated missiles, drones, and campus closures -- demonstrating the robustness of online infrastructure under extreme conditions.

Ubell's central claim: the 'safe space' in the article title is not political or ideological but literal -- online learning platforms provide cognitive and social continuity that physical campuses cannot guarantee in conflict.

The wartime use case reveals something important about the depth of the human need for education: even students experiencing trauma and displacement seek structured learning as a form of normalcy and resilience.

From a systems perspective, the success of wartime online learning validates design choices made for entirely different reasons -- accessibility and flexibility for peacetime edge cases that happen to be essential in extremis.
